name: Prevent and control infections (isolation cases and outbreaks)
function: quality, patient safety and infection prevention and control
summary: This process stops infections spreading inside the hospital. Infection prevention and control practitioners review new positive results and flagged admissions, make sure nurses have placed the right precautions, arrange single rooms and enhanced cleaning, trace exposed patients and staff, report diseases of public health significance and, when cases cluster, declare and run an outbreak with the public health unit. Each isolated patient is reviewed until precautions can stop or the patient goes home. It is slow and error-prone because practitioners work weekday hours while results arrive around the clock, single rooms are scarce, and outbreak work in respiratory season and the COVID-19 waves of 2020-2022 crowds out routine surveillance.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation of about 640 beds with a central IPAC team in the quality department, an IPAC physician lead and a regional public health unit.
baseline.notes: One case is one new isolation case or outbreak follow-up. Hand hygiene audits, education, product evaluation, construction risk assessments and COVID-19 screening programmes are part of the team's work but not case work.

unit_of_work: one isolation case or outbreak action
trigger: A positive laboratory result, an admission flagged with an organism, or a public health notice reaches the IPAC team.
end_state: Precautions are discontinued, the patient is discharged with the case closed, the outbreak is declared over, or no action is needed.

volume.seasonality: Peaks from December to March with influenza and RSV, and with COVID-19 waves in 2020-2022.

evidence.note: Author's estimate. At the provincial C. difficile rate of 0.20 per 1,000 inpatient days, about 18,500 patient days a month give about 4 hospital-acquired C. difficile cases a month; antibiotic-resistant organism carriers found on admission screening, respiratory viruses and other organisms make up most cases.

surge.cause: Winter respiratory virus season (influenza and RSV; COVID-19 waves from 2020)

evidence.note: Author's estimate matching the organisation file.

Ontario hospitals averaged 1 ICP per 90 beds (range 62 to 135) three years after SARS (bryce2008), about 7 for 640 beds; ICPs need 80 hours of endorsed training and CIC certification (pidac_rpap). The organisation file lists 12, consistent with COVID-19 era expansion; about 7 FTE on case work is the author's estimate.
Author's estimate: placing precautions and collecting screening and clearance swabs.
Author's estimate: single-room moves for isolation.
Author's estimate: staff exposure follow-up; much higher during COVID-19 waves.

roles.title: Director, quality, risk and patient experience
roles.department: Quality, patient safety and professional practice

evidence.note: Author's estimate: chairing outbreak meetings.
Author's estimate; Ontario hospitals usually have a physician lead for IPAC (an infectious diseases physician or medical microbiologist), often part-time or shared.

roles.title: IPAC physician lead (infectious diseases physician or medical microbiologist)

systems.name: Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Ontario Laboratories Information System and ConnectingOntario viewer
Electronic bed board and patient flow dashboard
Fax (referrals, requisitions and reports to community physicians)
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones

steps.name: Review daily alert list
steps.description: Each morning the infection prevention and control practitioner opens the list of new positive results (MRSA, VRE, CPE, C. difficile, influenza, COVID-19, tuberculosis and others) from the laboratory system and faxed or OLIS reference results, plus admissions flagged with an organism, and decides which need action.

next.condition: new case needing precautions or follow-up
already known and isolated, or not significant

evidence.note: Author's estimate: practitioners work weekday days with on-call cover, so results that arrive on Friday evening wait until Monday unless urgent.

steps.name: Check patient location and precautions
steps.description: The practitioner finds the patient's current room on the bed board, checks whether additional precautions are already ordered in the chart and phones the unit charge nurse to confirm signage and room type.

next.condition: precautions already started by the unit

evidence.note: PIDAC expects precautions to start at symptom onset or on ARO risk without waiting for laboratory confirmation, and any regulated professional may start them (pidac_rpap). The 65% share already in place is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Place additional precautions
steps.description: The patient's nurse posts the precaution sign at the door, sets up a PPE cart with gowns, gloves and masks, dedicates equipment such as a stethoscope and commode, and tells the patient and family what the precautions mean.

control.basis: PIDAC Routine Practices and Additional Precautions in All Health Care Settings (Public Health Ontario); Accreditation Canada infection prevention and control standards

evidence.note: Signage specific to the type of precautions and specialised accommodation (pidac_rpap). Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Verify precautions and flag the chart
steps.description: The practitioner confirms the type of precautions suits the organism, enters an organism alert in the hospital information system so it shows on future visits and adds the case to the isolation list used by bed management.

control.basis: PIDAC Routine Practices and Additional Precautions in All Health Care Settings (Public Health Ontario): ICP verification of additional precautions

next.condition: patient in a shared room; needs a single room
already in a single room or cohort acceptable

evidence.note: The designated practitioner must be informed when precautions are started and verifies they are appropriate (pidac_rpap). The share needing a move is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Find a single room and move patient
steps.description: The patient flow coordinator looks for a free single room on the bed board, negotiates with unit managers to swap patients if none is free, and books the move and the cleaning of the vacated bed.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; single rooms are scarce in older Ontario hospital wings and fill quickly in respiratory season.

steps.name: Request enhanced cleaning
steps.description: The practitioner asks environmental services to switch the room to enhanced or sporicidal cleaning, for example twice-daily cleaning for C. difficile, and to clean the vacated bed space if the patient moved.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Classify case and enter on line list
steps.description: The practitioner reviews admission date, symptom onset and earlier results in the chart to decide whether the infection is hospital-acquired under surveillance definitions, and enters the case in the surveillance spreadsheet used for monthly rates and public reporting.

error.defect_description: Case misclassified as hospital- or community-acquired.

control.basis: Ontario Ministry of Health public reporting of hospital patient safety indicators (C. difficile, MRSA/VRE bacteremia)

next.condition: roommates or staff may have been exposed

evidence.note: Ontario hospitals publicly report C. difficile and MRSA/VRE bloodstream infections per 1,000 inpatient days (provincial rates 0.20 and 0.037). The exposure share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Trace exposed patients and staff
steps.description: The practitioner lists roommates and patients who shared a bathroom or were on the unit during the infectious period, pulls staff assignments for airborne or unprotected exposures, and decides who needs screening or assessment.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Collect screening swabs from contacts
steps.description: The unit nurses collect nasal, rectal or respiratory swabs from the listed contacts under a medical directive, label them and send them to the laboratory, placing contacts on precautions until results return where policy requires.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess exposed staff
steps.description: The occupational health nurse contacts each exposed staff member, checks immunity and fit-test records, arranges baseline or follow-up testing and decides on any work restriction, telling the manager and scheduling office.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act (Ontario) and Regulation 67/93 (Health Care and Residential Facilities): employer duty to protect workers from infectious exposure

evidence.note: Author's estimate; for tuberculosis and measles exposures the work runs over weeks.

steps.name: Decide whether the case is reportable
steps.description: The practitioner checks the organism against the list of diseases of public health significance and looks for links to other recent cases on the same unit that could signal a cluster.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of the reportable share.

steps.name: Report to the public health unit
steps.description: The practitioner phones or faxes the regional public health unit with the case details on the provincial reporting form, answers the investigator's questions and records the report in the case file.

control.basis: Health Protection and Promotion Act (Ontario): hospital duty to report diseases of public health significance to the medical officer of health

next.condition: public health or IPAC sees a possible cluster

evidence.note: Author's estimate of minutes per report.

steps.name: IPAC physician reviews possible cluster
steps.description: The IPAC physician lead reviews the line list with the practitioner, compares onset dates and locations against outbreak case definitions and, with the public health unit, decides whether to declare an outbreak.

control.basis: Health Protection and Promotion Act (Ontario): institutional outbreaks declared and managed with the medical officer of health

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Convene outbreak management team
steps.description: The director of quality chairs the first outbreak meeting with IPAC, the unit manager, environmental services, occupational health, patient flow and public health, agreeing on admissions closure, visiting limits, staff cohorting and communication.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Review isolated patient for discontinuation
steps.description: Each day the practitioner reviews patients on the isolation list against discontinuation criteria such as 48 hours without diarrhea for C. difficile or the end of the infectious period, and notes who is about to be discharged.

next.condition: patient discharged while still on precautions

evidence.note: Precautions stay until there is no longer a risk of transmission and are discontinued in consultation with the ICP (pidac_rpap). Shares and timing are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Run the outbreak
steps.description: Two practitioners keep the daily line list, send it to public health, swab new symptomatic patients, audit PPE and hand hygiene on the unit, update signage and admission restrictions and report to the outbreak team until no new cases appear.

control.basis: Health Protection and Promotion Act (Ontario): outbreak reporting to the medical officer of health

next.condition: no new cases for the required period

evidence.note: Author's estimate: minutes are the total for one practitioner across the outbreak; two practitioners share the work.

steps.name: Public health declares outbreak over
steps.description: The public health unit reviews the final line list and declares the outbreak over once two incubation periods have passed without new cases; the hospital then reopens the unit to admissions.

evidence.note: Author's estimate: respiratory outbreaks usually last two to four weeks.

steps.name: Collect clearance swabs
steps.description: The unit nurse collects the follow-up swabs needed to clear an antibiotic-resistant organism, on the schedule set by policy, and sends them to the laboratory; precautions stay until the results are back.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; clearance schedules for MRSA and VRE take one to three weeks.

steps.name: Discontinue precautions
steps.description: The practitioner tells the unit and the attending physician that precautions can stop, removes or updates the organism alert in the chart and requests a discharge-level clean of the room before the next patient.

control.basis: PIDAC Routine Practices and Additional Precautions in All Health Care Settings (Public Health Ontario): discontinuation in consultation with the ICP

evidence.note: The attending physician should be notified when precautions are discontinued; if the ICP and physician disagree, the higher level stays (pidac_rpap).

steps.name: Close case at discharge
steps.description: When an isolated patient is discharged, the practitioner checks that the organism alert stays on the chart, that the receiving long-term care home or hospital is told, and that environmental services do a terminal clean of the room.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Outbreak declared
exceptions.description: Linked cases on a unit lead to an outbreak with admission closure, daily line lists to public health and two to four weeks of extra work.

exceptions.name: Staff exposure
exceptions.description: An unprotected exposure (tuberculosis, measles, COVID-19) means occupational health assesses and may restrict staff.

exceptions.name: No single room
exceptions.description: The patient waits in a shared room with precautions until a single room or swap is found.

exceptions.name: Clearance swabs
exceptions.description: An antibiotic-resistant organism carrier stays on precautions through a series of clearance swabs, often longer than the stay.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from positive result to precautions discontinued, discharge or outbreak closed
benchmarks.population: Isolation cases in a community hospital

evidence.note: Author's estimate: isolation usually lasts the rest of the stay (about four to five days after the positive result) or the infectious period; no published distribution was found.
Range 1 ICP per 62 to 135 beds; British Columbia median 1 per 175.
MRSA/VRE bloodstream infections 0.037 per 1,000 inpatient days.

pain_points.description: Practitioners work weekday days while results arrive around the clock, so cases found on Friday evening wait for Monday unless the unit calls.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Single rooms are scarce, so isolation patients wait in shared rooms or block beds while swaps are negotiated.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Surveillance line lists and public health reports are kept in spreadsheets and sent by fax and phone, re-keying the same case details several times.

evidence.note: Author's estimate for 2019-2022.

pain_points.description: Outbreaks in respiratory season and the COVID-19 waves take two practitioners for weeks and push routine surveillance and audits aside.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

assumptions: One case is one new isolation case; an outbreak is reached from a case and its work is counted on that case.
The IPAC physician lead is added because the organisation file has no such role.
ICP stated FTE (7 of 12) covers case work only; audits, education, construction reviews and COVID-19 screening and vaccination programmes take the rest.
s16 minutes are one practitioner's total over the whole outbreak, with two practitioners (people = 2).
The wait before s15 is the time until the patient meets discontinuation criteria, the length of the infectious period or stay, not a queue.
The touch-time check implies about 3.7 FTE against 10.4 stated; the difference is daily rounds on isolated patients beyond the logged minutes, and audit and education time linked to cases.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file; the IPAC physician cost is set like a department chief.
